prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. No member disputes that the flat-band prediction (2011) and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states (2018) are real and reproduced by many groups. The system turns a strongly correlated many-body problem into something controlled by one parameter, the twist angle, and it has already spread to fractional Chern insulators and other moire platforms. B017 was in the top three of five members with different specialities, which says something about breadth, although I do not treat counts as merit. I also agree with the chair's observation that B015 and B017 are both secure; the question is which is the better prize. I judge that a discovery that opened a new regime of physics weighs somewhat more than a measurement invention of comparable quality, and I accept that reasonable members can weigh it the other way.
statement.case_against: Three objections remain. First, maturity: the discovery is eight years old and the pairing mechanism is open. I still think this is an interpretation question, but the citation must stay with the prediction and the observation of the states and must not claim an explanation. Second, attribution: Yuan Cao as first author, the Dean, Young, Kim and Yazdani groups and earlier twisted-bilayer band theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) sit outside the three names, and no citation wording repairs that; it is the real cost of this configuration. Third, the B015 camp has a genuinely cleaner credit story (two names, no forced exclusion), and I cannot dismiss the argument that a prize with fewer contested boundaries is the safer scientific judgment.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes (magic wavelength, many atoms in parallel) and warns that we should not read agreement among instrument-minded members as merit.
responses.response: I accept the distinctness argument; I no longer regard overlap with 2005 and 2012 as a strong objection to B015, and I keep it as my first alternative. Our remaining difference is the criterion the chair raised: whether a prize should go first to a new regime of physics or to a new measurement capability. The clock's payoff, tests of constants and dark matter and a redefinition of the second, is still partly prospective, while moire matter is already being built on by groups far from its origin. Kroll's point about field-correlated enthusiasm cuts both ways, and as a statistical physicist near this field I discount my own enthusiasm for B017 in the same way. Kroll also raised doubt about my first-round choice, B003; that criticism is fair, and the lack of any support for it is why I no longer prefer it.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that B017 has a harder attribution problem than the clock, with experimental credit spread over several groups, and that it is broader in reach but not riper.
responses.response: I agree that B017 is the less tidy of the two on credit, and I list that as my main case against. I disagree that it is less ripe in the sense that matters for a discovery prize: the existence of the correlated and superconducting states has been reproduced by independent groups in several device geometries, which is the same standard applied to the clock. Her reading of B003 as mainly cell biology, with the physics credit not separable in a three-name physics prize, is persuasive, and it is the reason I move B003 out of my alternatives.

responses.point: Johansson accepts that the discovery is robust but is less relaxed about maturity, wants a citation built on the prediction and the observation of the phases without claims about their origin, and keeps Bistritzer as a joint author.
responses.response: We agree on the citation, and I have kept its wording to the prediction and the observation of the states. I have also dropped the phrase about opening the field of moire quantum matter, since it points at the wider twistronics work, including Cao and the other groups, which the three names do not cover. On Bistritzer I agree with her that the 2011 continuum model was a joint paper and that omitting him would give MacDonald credit that belongs to the pair.

responses.point: Eriksson would credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero for B017 and prefers B051, citing a two-decade record of confirmation.
responses.response: The two-name option is defensible and I still accept it if the committee wants a compact citation, but I keep three because a prize for the prediction would then omit one of the two authors of that prediction, and the three-name limit leaves room for him. On B051 I accept that it is the most mature candidate; my difficulty remains that the 2D and 3D parts and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal make the credit boundary harder to defend than for B017, even though B017 also has omissions. I do not think the 2016 topological-phases prize is the decisive obstacle for B051 that others suggest, and for B017 the 2010 graphene prize concerned a different discovery.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the maturity test applied to B017 should be applied to the pulsar-timing background (B004) on the same footing.
responses.response: I agree on consistency of the criterion. I ranked B004 in my opening ballot and would not now hold B017 to a stricter standard than a 3-4 sigma background from individual arrays, though I also accept that B004 is not a serious competitor this year. I do not follow Danielsson in treating the open pairing mechanism as irrelevant to the citation: it is irrelevant to whether the discovery is secure, but it is the reason the citation should be limited to what is observed.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the omission of Yuan Cao and the other experimental groups under the three-name limit, or whether that weakens B017 against the clean two-name B015.
Whether three names or two is right for B017; I keep three but would accept MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero only.
Whether the unresolved superconducting mechanism leads colleagues to prefer waiting, which would favour B015 this year and B017 later.
Whether I weigh the opening of a new field above a measurement invention for reasons that are scientific or merely reflect my own field of correlated many-body physics.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional connection to MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori, Ye or the other credited names is documented in my profile. My field, statistical physics of complex systems, is adjacent to correlated-electron physics and was closest to the condensate candidate B003, which I no longer prefer; this is field affinity only. I note the disclosures made by Johansson-Goran (B012), Olsson-Eva, Lindroth-Eva and Kroll-Stefan and see no reason for recusal on B017 or B015.
